summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation, and the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. Sexual-orientation discrimination was banned in 1996, making South Africa the first country to do so; marriage equality followed with the Civil Union Act of 2006; legal gender recognition has been available since the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003; and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075), a challenge brought against the Department of Correctional Services with the assistance of Lawyers for Human Rights. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate prescribed gender-affirming health care falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. Orders compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and deliver prescribed medical care were granted. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling the same day.

Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling; reporting in August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice. Detention therefore remains a site of elevated risk for trans visitors and residents despite the binding remedies now in place.

Outside prison, everyday exposure is shaped by documents. The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act requires medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks people out of legal gender recognition, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people altogether; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Costs of affirming one's gender through the process are described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report documents a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

Violence risk is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month. Violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven. Activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 examining whether the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution prohibits the exclusion of transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.

Within North West province, the principal sub-national legal divergence is the reach of traditional and customary courts. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the former-Bantustan geography, which includes North West, as standing under a separate legal system; HRW's earlier reporting on the Traditional Courts Bill (29 May 2012) described a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans, offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction, and recorded that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, with chiefs' courts punishing lesbians in rural areas. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended, and the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law, and no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

Healthcare access is the sharpest practical constraint on the ground. The trans community in North West cannot access hormone replacement therapy at any public health facility in the province; the North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people in response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the South African Human Rights Commission, and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to obtain it. A visitor dependent on prescribed HRT should expect no provincial public provider and should carry a sufficient supply.

Hate-crime evidence for the province is thin but exists. The Love Not Hate campaign research conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being (2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study covering Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and the national campaign study itself. North West is therefore one of only three provinces ever to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study.
tangentialFactors:
North West's evidence base rests largely on a single province-level survey. 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province', released in October 2010, reported a survey conducted during 2009 and 2010 under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology, with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella collaborating, covering 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces. Questions addressed openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination. Findings beyond that scope are not carried in this record.

Institutional enforcement of gendered norms is documented at school level: on 23 March 2016 MambaOnline, citing the Taung Daily News, reported that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt, the principal sending her home with the instruction that she must wear a skirt 'since I was a girl'. She stayed home for three weeks without attending classes. The case is a single data point on a socially conservative enforcement climate rather than a rule binding visitors.

HRW's 2012 reporting positioned the Traditional Courts Bill as threatening LGBT South Africans specifically by removing the option to decline customary jurisdiction, against a documented background of poor police cooperation in rural areas; that framing predates the 2023 Mogale invalidation and the delayed TKLB, so the current practical reach of chiefs' courts over gender and sexual matters in North West is not established by these sources.

Residents of North West seeking hormone replacement therapy must leave the province. The North West Department of Health has confirmed that no facility in the province provides HRT for transgender people, and people travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng for treatment. The confirmation came in the Department's response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the South African Human Rights Commission, which remains the route used to press the provincial health authority on this gap.

Legal gender recognition runs through the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, which demands medical evidence, restricts classification to a binary, and carries costs described as dauntingly high; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. Non-binary residents cannot obtain a matching marker. Where identity documents conflict with presentation, residents report denial of service, humiliation and threats of arrest for alleged fraud, and the Gender Dynamix reporting includes a trans woman refused when filing a domestic-violence complaint.

Residents in rural parts of the province may fall within customary-law adjudication under the traditional leadership framework, an arrangement HRW characterises as a separate legal system with no opt-out; the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended pending the delayed replacement Bill. Provincial schooling has enforced gendered dress codes against gender-nonconforming pupils, as the 2016 Maphoitsile village case shows.

Local research capacity exists: the 2010 province survey was run by the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella, and North West was one of three provinces covered by a dedicated hate-crime prevalence study.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the North West Department of Health has established any HRT provision since the February 2023 report and the subsequent South African Human Rights Commission complaint; no later source is available here.

Unresolved: whether chiefs' courts in North West are currently adjudicating gender and sexual matters in practice, and how the 2023 Mogale suspension and the delayed TKLB have altered day-to-day jurisdiction. The HRW material describing punishment of lesbians in chiefs' courts dates from 2012.

Unresolved: the outcome of the 2016 school dress-code case involving Zinzi Manini Molema, including whether she was readmitted or any disciplinary or equality complaint followed.

Not sourced: the substantive findings of the 2010 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province' survey beyond its design and sample of 319 respondents, and the province-specific hate-crime figures in the Love Not Hate study. Neither document's results are carried here.

Not sourced: any North West-specific incidence of anti-trans violence with a named victim and date comparable to the Tshwane and national figures recorded elsewhere in this dossier.
